1.title: The Progress Practice
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: The Progress Practice. It covers the exam area The prince two practices. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Explain the purpose of the progress practice and its relationships with the principles. Explain the purpose of the checkpoint, highlight, end stage, end project, lessons and exception reports, the daily log, the lessons log and the digital and data management approach. Define forecast, exception, tolerance and event-driven and time-driven controls. Describe tolerances, types of control, reviewing and reporting progress and lessons, forecasting, escalating and the use of data and systems. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The prince two practices (sixty percent). Exam format: sixty multiple-choice questions in sixty minutes; thirty-six correct answers (sixty percent) pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Foundation syllabus (people cert).

1.title: Purpose
1.text: Purpose. The progress practice sets up mechanisms to monitor and compare actual achievements with those planned, to forecast the project's objectives and continued viability, and to control unacceptable deviations.

1.title: Key concepts
1.text: Key concepts. Forecast. A prediction of future performance or results. Tolerance. The permissible deviation above and below a plan's target before escalation is needed. Exception. A situation where a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. Event-driven control. Control that happens when something occurs (end of a stage, an exception). Time-driven control. Control that happens at regular intervals (a weekly or monthly report).

1.title: Tolerance levels and escalation
1.text: Tolerance levels and escalation. The figure shows this: Tolerances and escalation: team manager to project manager to project board to corporate level.

1.title: Tolerance levels and escalation, continued
1.text: Tolerance levels and escalation. Project. Who sets tolerance: Corporate or programme management (to the project board). Escalate to: Corporate or programme. Stage. Who sets tolerance: Project board (to the project manager). Escalate to: Project board. Work package. Who sets tolerance: Project manager (to the team manager). Escalate to: Project manager. Exam tip: If a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, it is an exception: escalate to the next level up. The board is told through an exception report.

1.title: Reports and records
1.text: Reports and records. Checkpoint report. From to: team manager to project manager. Type: time-driven. Purpose: Progress of a work package. Highlight report. From to: project manager to board. Type: time-driven. Purpose: Stage progress at regular intervals. End stage report. From to: project manager to board. Type: event-driven. Purpose: Stage results and a view of the next. End project report. From to: project manager to board. Type: event-driven. Purpose: Review of the whole project at closure. Lessons report. From to: project manager. Type: event-driven. Purpose: Lessons for use by others.

1.title: Reports and records, continued
1.text: Reports and records. Exception report. From to: project manager to board. Type: event-driven. Purpose: Describes an exception, options and a recommendation. Daily log (project log). From to: project manager. Type: ongoing. Purpose: Informal notes and items not captured elsewhere. Lessons log (project log). From to: project manager. Type: ongoing. Purpose: All useful lessons as they appear. Digital and data management approach (P I D). From to: project manager. Type: at initiation. Purpose: How data and digital tools are used and protected. Exam tip: Checkpoint equals team to project manager. Highlight equals project manager to board, at intervals. End stage and exception reports are event-driven.

1.title: Progress guidance
1.text: Progress guidance. Tolerances for progress control. Set tolerances for time, cost, quality, scope, benefits, risk, sustainability at each level. Types of control. Time-driven and event-driven controls, at the board and project manager levels. Reviewing progress and lessons. Compare actual with plan; learn as you go. Reporting progress and lessons. Communicate status to the right people at the right time. Forecasting. Predict outcomes so action is early. Escalating. Raise an exception to the next level promptly. Use of data and systems. Digital tools and data to track and report progress. Exam tip: A tolerance is the allowed deviation; an exception is when it is forecast to be exceeded. Escalate as soon as it is forecast, not after it happens.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A team manager reports progress on a work package to the project manager every week. Which report is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Checkpoint report. A checkpoint report goes from a team manager to the project manager.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which statements are C O R R E C T? (one) A highlight report goes from the project manager to the board. (two) An exception report is event-driven. (three) A checkpoint report goes from the board to the project manager. (four) An end stage report is time-driven. The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: one and two. Highlight goes to the board, and an exception report is event-driven.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Identify the missing word. An blank occurs when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Exception. That is an exception.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which control happens at regular intervals? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Time-driven. Time-driven controls happen at regular intervals.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. The project manager forecasts a stage will exceed its cost tolerance. What should happen? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Raise an exception to the project board. Escalate the exception to the board.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Where are useful lessons recorded as they come up? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: The lessons log. The lessons log collects lessons throughout.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Define a tolerance. Answer: The permissible deviation above and below a plan's target before escalation is needed. Question two. What is an exception? Answer: A situation where a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. Question three. Who produces the highlight report and who receives it? Answer: The project manager produces it for the project board.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Name two event-driven reports. Answer: The end stage report and the exception report. Question five. What does the daily log hold? Answer: Informal notes and items not captured in other products. Question six. Which product describes how data and digital tools are used and protected? Answer: The digital and data management approach.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Tolerance or exception: permitted deviation or tolerance forecast to be exceeded. Controls: time-driven (regular) and event-driven. Reports: checkpoint, highlight, end stage, end project, lessons, exception. Logs: daily log and lessons log (project log). Escalation: to the next level up.
